Crossing Sideways

[1] As soon as my kayak left the sheltered cove, the current pushed its bow downstream. [2] On the final morning of a paddling course, our group would cross a narrow channel to a gravel bar. [3] I had practiced stopping and turning on still water, so I expected to point directly at the bar and paddle across.[1]

Our instructor, Maya, demonstrated first. She attacked[2] the moving water with her bow angled upstream. Her paddle kept a steady rhythm, the kayak traveled diagonally and reached the bar without being swept below it.[3] From shore, the maneuver looked almost ordinary.

At Maya's signal, I aimed at the gravel bar itself. Each stroke moved me forward, but the current carried me sideways faster than I realized. Maya pointed to a pale boulder on the opposite bank and told me to watch whether it shifted behind my bow.[4] Each paddler could use their[5] chosen landmark to see drift that was difficult to feel from the boat.

I turned back before reaching the main channel. By then, I had went[6] far enough downstream to understand why greater effort in the same direction would not solve the problem. Maya asked me to choose an upstream angle with the aim of possibly managing to[7] balance the current. A line of bubbles beside the kayak were[8] moving steadily toward the bend.

[A] I studied the boulder again. [B] This time, I pointed the bow several degrees upstream from the gravel bar.[9] [C] I paddled at the same pace I had used in the cove, checking the boulder after every few strokes. [D] The bow still moved sideways, but now the sideways movement carried me toward the landing instead of past it. When the hull touched gravel, I laughed at how little the crossing had resembled a straight line.

On still water, the place I aimed and the place I traveled had seemed identical. The current separated those ideas. I crossed successfully only after treating drift as information and choosing an angle that accounted for it. Sometimes the most direct progress begins by pointing somewhere other than the visible destination.[10]
